prize_parts.citation: for the detection of high-energy astrophysical neutrinos with a cubic-kilometre detector in Antarctic ice, opening neutrino astronomy
for the development of optical lattice clocks reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18

statement.case_for: I keep IceCube first and add the lattice clocks as the second part. IceCube is a detector-driven discovery: a cubic kilometre of Antarctic ice instrumented to see Cherenkov light from neutrinos, a diffuse astrophysical flux established in 2013 and confirmed in several independent channels, then the blazar TXS 0506+056, NGC 1068 and the Galactic plane. This is a new observational window of the kind that has historically carried the prize. The optical lattice clock is the cleanest precision-measurement result on the list. Katori's magic-wavelength proposal and first demonstration, and Ye's work taking strontium to 10^-18 with careful systematics control, have been reproduced at JILA, RIKEN and Tokyo, NIST, PTB and SYRTE, and underpin tests of relativity and constants and the coming redefinition of the second. The two parts are distinct achievements, and the three names (Halzen, Katori, Ye) fit the statutory limit. The configuration also pairs the two candidates that drew the most first-place and top-three support from people who ranked neither B020 nor B021 first, which gives a realistic route to a consensus.
statement.case_against: The weakest point is attribution in B052. The credited string names only Halzen, and an experiment of this size rests on instrument builders and analysis leaders who are not on the list; if the committee judges that a fair IceCube prize needs a different set of names, B052 loses force and the config would have to change. Source identification (NGC 1068, the Galactic plane) is also still at moderate significance, so some may call the astronomy half premature. Against B024, Hall, Hansch and Wineland already sit close in prize history, and priority for the lattice clock is not uncontested. Pairing neutrino astronomy with clocks also has no thematic unity, and a committee that wants one coherent prize may prefer a single part such as B025 or B020.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks B025 (BeppoSAX afterglows, Costa, Frontera, Kulkarni) first as a true discovery of nature, and B052 second, noting that the single credited name for IceCube is administratively clean but may not capture the collaboration.
responses.response: I agree with Ulf that B025 is a fully mature discovery and I ranked it second, so I will not leave it. I share his attribution worry on B052 and think it is the strongest reason not to push IceCube as a solo prize. Where I differ is on whether B025 should be preferred outright. Its credit has three names that already use the whole three-person budget, which leaves no room for a second achievement, and I worry that the optical-identification credit (the van Paradijs and Groot team) is more open than the BeppoSAX instrument credit. I therefore keep B025 as my first alternative and would support it if the committee wants one astrophysics prize and cannot settle the IceCube names.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first, as a measurement instrument that redefines what can be measured, with Katori and Ye a clean pair and many independent labs reproducing 10^-18 performance.
responses.response: I accept Stefan's case and moved B024 into my preferred configuration as a distinct second part, because I judge the experimental case to be the best on the list in terms of calibration, systematics and independent confirmation. My reservation is the same one I raised in my opening: Hall, Hansch and Wineland (2005, 2012) already sit near it, so I would want the citation to rest on the lattice and the 10^-18 uncertainty, not on frequency metrology in general. I would like Stefan to say whether he thinks the Katori-Ye split is robust against the Lemonde and Gill priority argument.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks twisted bilayer graphene (B021) first for the Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction and the Jarillo-Herrero experiments, and B016 second, and notes the superconducting pairing is still debated.
responses.response: The Bistritzer-MacDonald prediction followed by experiment is a clean story, and I do not dismiss it. But Olle himself says the pairing mechanism is unsettled, and Danielsson would take only MacDonald and Jarillo-Herrero, so the three-name credit is contested even among supporters. As a non-specialist in condensed matter I defer to him on the physics, but I would ask him whether the central discovery will still look the same in ten years. On my criterion of independent confirmation with understood systematics, B021 is still less mature than the clock or neutrino results, so I do not place it in my configuration.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks optical-lattice quantum simulation (B020) first, as a measurable realisation of the Hubbard model with single-site resolution, and B024 second for its theory-measurement agreement.
responses.response: Eva's support for B024 helps my configuration, and I take her point that the lattice clock is an area where theory and measurement agree to extreme precision. On B020 I defer to her and to Johansson on the atomic physics. My concern is that five credited names have to be cut to three and that Cirac and Zoller appear under B006 as well, so the credit is crowded; Eva's own trio swaps Esslinger for Zoller, which differs from Kroll's and Johansson's, which shows the allocation is open. I keep B020 as an alternative, not as the preferred part.

uncertainties: Whether the committee can accept a one-name IceCube prize, or whether the instrument-builder credit makes B052 unworkable under the three-laureate limit.
Whether pairing neutrino astronomy with atomic clocks reads as an acceptable two-part prize or as an arbitrary combination.
How much the 2005 and 2012 prizes narrow the room for B024.
Whether the BeppoSAX and optical-afterglow credit split in B025 can be defended against the van Paradijs and Groot team.
I rely on memory for IceCube and clock milestones, and I defer to colleagues on atomic and condensed-matter attribution.
statement.conflict_note: My profile shows I work in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations. I have no collaboration or institutional tie to the IceCube or optical-clock candidates or to the credited names, but my own astroparticle background is close to B052 and B025, so I would ask colleagues to weigh my views there with that in mind. No specific conflict requiring recusal is apparent from the provided profile.
